documents: Published paper: Wilson & McCrory (2022), Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 23, e2022GC010442 (PDF, 23 pp.)

entry.evidence: The literature is remarkably silent on how the ∼100 km northward component of motion

steps.action: Take from published Basin and Range and paleomagnetic reconstructions that the northern Sierra Nevada moved WNW (~200 km W, ~100 km N) and Oregon rotated 15–20° clockwise since the early Miocene.
steps.quote: the northern Sierra Nevada has moved west-northwest relative to the Colorado plateau since the early Miocene

steps.action: Derive from these accepted motions that Washington must have absorbed at least ~100 km of N-S convergence, illustrated in a schematic reconstruction (Figure 2).
steps.quote: Accepting the relationships above requires large strains in Washington since the early Miocene

steps.action: Pose the question of how this ~100 km northward motion is distributed as fault offsets, since few Washington faults are thought to have more than 10 km offset.
steps.quote: The literature is remarkably silent on how the ∼100 km northward component of motion

steps.action: State the aim of offering one regionally complete strain-history hypothesis, conditional on the consensus motions of Oregon and the Sierra Nevada being correct.
steps.quote: The purpose of this paper is to offer a regionally complete hypothesis for strain history of greater Cascadia since early Miocene

steps.action: Choose kinematic modeling of rigid microplates, made to fit geodesy and seismicity at the young end and to place as much motion as practical on recognized faults.
steps.quote: We use kinematic modeling of rigid microplates as an illustration tool.

steps.action: Compile published GPS velocities, earthquake catalogs, CRBG stratigraphy and ages, YFTB structure, Ginkgo paleomagnetic declinations, and Puget Lowland and Seattle fault geophysics (Figures 3-6).
steps.quote: Geodetic results in this area (McCaffrey et al., 2013; Payne et al., 2012) show westward motion and clockwise rotation

steps.action: Build the block model as finite rotations on a sphere (technique after Wilson et al. 2005), with a Pacific-North America plate-circuit boundary condition, motion changes at 12.5 and 5.9 Ma, and block rotation parameters (Table 1, Tables S1-S3, Movie S1).
steps.quote: block motions described by finite rotations on a sphere in exactly the same manner as the rotations of major plates

steps.action: Revise the model over many iterations after early versions had faults alternating between right- and left-lateral or compressive and extensional motion; the unsuccessful models are not shown.
steps.quote: Model development has gone through many generations of iteration.

steps.action: Compare the model's restored rotations with paleomagnetic declinations of the Ginkgo (~16 Ma) and Pomona (~11 Ma) basalts; restoring the rotations reduces declination scatter (Figure 8).
steps.quote: The clockwise rotations restored in the reconstructions dramatically reduce scatter in the declinations.

steps.action: Explain the smaller differential rotation of Pomona by a reassigned age (~11 Ma, from an Ar-loss argument), so that rotation predates eruption, and by different sampling distributions; slight rotation is added in southeastern Washington.
steps.quote: We interpret the difference in relative rotation between the two units here to two major factors.

steps.action: Compare the modeled YFTB shortening (47 km at 120°W) with published minimum shortening and strike-slip offsets, and the implied ≥60 km Cascade Range shortening with seismicity and focal mechanisms.
steps.quote: Recent seismicity is fully consistent with this interpretation

steps.action: Favor low-angle thrust sheets over high-angle reverse faults for the Puget Lowland, and oroclinal shortening over an original arcuate shape for the Olympic Peninsula, on the grounds of the large required shortening.
steps.quote: Our interpretation is that the large amount of total shortening is much more plausibly accommodated on low-angle thrust sheets.

steps.action: Check model elements against regional constraints in north-central and south-central Oregon, the Walker Lane (Faulds offsets, Carson domain rotation), the Klamath Mountains, the Oregon-Idaho graben and the Snake River Plain (Figure 10).
steps.quote: We found it straightforward to implement the interpretation of progressive eastward motion of a deformation boundary

steps.action: Estimate Sierra Nevada motion (228 km at 296° since 17 Ma) along an independent northern path through Oregon, and compare it with the southern-transect estimate of McQuarrie & Wernicke (235 ± 20 km at 282°).
steps.quote: Our estimate of SNGV motion appears to agree very well with that of McQuarrie and Wernicke (2005).

steps.action: Adjust the youngest model step (2.6-0 Ma) to fit GPS velocities, noting that the fit is not a test given the model's degrees of freedom (Figure 12a).
steps.quote: Our kinematic model has been adjusted such that velocities for the youngest time step (2.6–0 Ma) agree closely with geodetic results

steps.action: Compare the modeled velocity history, with changes near 6 and 12.5 Ma, against published Basin and Range and plate-motion chronologies (Figures 12b-d).
steps.quote: Sensible progression of the model velocities through time can potentially be considered as evidence that the model captures important features

steps.action: Compare permanent deformation in southern Oregon and northern California with McCaffrey et al.'s model pn2d: this model has 1.3 mm/yr extension near Klamath Falls and a westward component more than 3 mm/yr faster.
steps.quote: We suggest that the issue of permanent deformation in southern Oregon is worth revisiting.

steps.action: Subtract upper-plate motion from Juan de Fuca-North America motion to estimate a uniform convergence of ~31 mm/yr at N61°E for 41-46°N (Figure 13), and derive current slip rates across the Cascades and Puget Lowland faults.
steps.quote: our model has convergence across the subduction zone from 41°N to 46°N at a speed of 31 mm/yr and an azimuth of 61°

steps.action: Qualify the assumption that the Devils Mountain Fault is the northern limit of deformation: 5-10 km of motion farther north would make the 94 km Puget estimate a slight overestimate without changing the conclusion.
steps.quote: This assumption is much more a matter of absence of evidence of permanent deformation than it is a matter of evidence of absence.

steps.action: Retain the model as a plausible, integrated framework, with Oregon rotating ~1°/Myr, YFTB and Puget Lowland shortening amounts, and many Washington faults to be considered seismically active.
steps.quote: The model demonstrates the plausibility that deformation on currently active faults has been ongoing since about 12 Ma at rates indicated by modern geodesy

tree.answer: Yes: at least 100 km of convergence across Washington, implied by accepted reconstructions
No; fault offsets are inferred from traces (paleomagnetism, structure, offsets) and from geodesy
Distribute the implied deformation across individual faults in a regionally complete model
No rival whole-region models; only local rivals (Puget fault geometry, Olympic orocline versus original shape)
Not computed; local rivals are judged by plausibility
Conditions found: past deformation known from traces
Partly: an independent northern-path estimate of Sierra Nevada motion agrees with McQuarrie & Wernicke; the GPS fit is tuned
Kept as a geologically plausible model

end.claim: The at least 100 km of Washington convergence implied by Oregon's clockwise rotation and Sierra Nevada translation can be accommodated in a geologically reasonable fault model: 47 km of shortening across the YFTB at 120°W, 94 km across the Puget Lowland (40 km on the Seattle Fault), and 125 km between Corvallis and Bellingham.

decisive_move.sentence: The claim exists only because the authors built and iteratively tuned a rigid-microplate finite-rotation model, constrained by paleomagnetism, geodesy and fault offsets, that assigns the required convergence to specific faults.

gates.evidence: The paper states "This paper contains no original data" (p. 20); all inputs are compiled. The GPS fit is tuned and "should not be considered impressive" (p. 16). The only comparison that could have failed is the independent northern-path Sierra Nevada motion against McQuarrie & Wernicke (2005) (p. 16). Nothing was fixed in advance, and the many unsuccessful iterations are not shown (p. 9).

novelty_claims.quote: [...] model offers a first detailed proposal of how late Cenozoic deformation is distributed across Washington
This study offers a reconstruction model as a first effort to propose a regionally complete summary of how this deformation could be distributed

limits: No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments mention reviews that improved the manuscript, but their content is unknown. The model is explicitly conditional on the consensus motions of Oregon and the Sierra Nevada being correct. The many unsuccessful model iterations are not shown, and the authors say they could not show the constraints those models offer. Uncertainties are subjective (about 20 km N-S and 40 km E-W for the Sierra Nevada motion) and no formal error propagation is given; partitioning among adjacent faults is poorly constrained. The GPS agreement is a fit, not a test. No rival region-wide distribution model is stated, so best_explanation is relative to implicit alternatives (inference). Internal inconsistency: the abstract and section 4.2 give 47 km of YFTB shortening at 120°W, but the conclusions give 37 km (p. 20). Sub-claims: the convergence of ~31 mm/yr at N61°E (estimate_with_resolution, though no uncertainty is stated); the Sierra Nevada motion of 228 km at 296° (estimate_with_resolution, subjective uncertainty); present-day slip rates on Cascade and Puget faults (estimate_with_resolution, weakly constrained); the suggestion that the Olympia Fault is possibly active (best_explanation, speculative).

disagreements.target: McCaffrey et al. (2013) block model pn2d
disagreements.support: The model has 1.3 mm/yr extension near Klamath Falls and a westward component more than 3 mm/yr faster in northern coastal California, supported by Quaternary normal faulting and focal mechanisms.
disagreements.quote: We suggest that the issue of permanent deformation in southern Oregon is worth revisiting.

disagreements.target: Uniform-dip high-angle reverse faults in the Puget Lowland (Brocher et al., 2001) and more complicated geometry (Brocher et al., 2004)
disagreements.support: The large total shortening the model requires is argued to be more plausibly accommodated on low-angle thrust sheets.
disagreements.quote: Our interpretation is that the large amount of total shortening is much more plausibly accommodated on low-angle thrust sheets.

disagreements.target: Published Washington fault offset estimates (few faults with more than 10 km offset)
disagreements.support: The model requires 94 km of Puget Lowland shortening, 40 km of it on the Seattle Fault, far above the published minimum offsets.
disagreements.quote: [...] have been suggested to have more than 10 km of offset

disagreements.target: Reidel et al. (1989) minimum YFTB shortening of ~40 km at 120°W
disagreements.support: The paleomagnetically constrained model gives 47 km, argued to be consistent with minimum estimates given listric fault geometry.
disagreements.quote: Our reconstruction, conforming to the paleomagnetic results discussed above, has slightly more shortening since 17 Ma, 47 km at 120°W

disagreements.target: Commonly quoted 12.0 Ma K-Ar age of the Pomona Member
disagreements.support: Using the 40Ar/39Ar plateau ages of Barry et al. (2013) and an argument that Ar loss explains discordant dates, they assign ~11 Ma.
disagreements.quote: we assign an age of about 11 Ma to the Pomona Member

disagreements.target: View that the arcuate shape of the Olympic Peninsula basement is original
disagreements.support: The westward increase in required N-S shortening leaves no practical alternative to deformation within the Olympic Peninsula.
disagreements.quote: We see no practical alternatives to assigning most of this shortening to deformation within the Olympic Peninsula

alternatives_considered.chosen: Walker Lane/eastern California shear zone initiation at 12.5 Ma
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 10 Ma (Snow & Wernicke, 2000), 12 Ma (Busby, 2013), possibly 13 Ma (Dokka & Travis, 1990)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Pomona Member age of about 11 Ma
alternatives_considered.alternatives: K-Ar dates of 14-8 Ma; 12.0 Ma most commonly quoted; 40Ar/39Ar ages of 11.21 and 10.34 Ma
alternatives_considered.reason: Ar loss during alteration taken as the most common cause of discordant 40Ar/39Ar dates

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Uniform-dip high-angle reverse faults; more complicated geometry
alternatives_considered.reason: Large total shortening more plausibly accommodated on low-angle thrusts

alternatives_considered.chosen: Most coastal shortening assigned to deformation within the Olympic Peninsula
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Original arcuate shape; [...] on submerged NW-SE faults in the Strait of Juan de Fuca (given lesser motion)
alternatives_considered.reason: N-S shortening must increase westward through Washington
